name: Zoe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the marketing team at Brightwell Home, the kettle and toaster brand. I look after small kitchen appliances, so I plan the campaigns for each new model, write the box copy and the instruction leaflet intros, and brief the photographers. Twice a month I'm at the big electrical stores checking how our shelves look.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is the store visits. Seeing a family pick up our kettle because the box told them what they needed to know, that's satisfying. The worst is the spreadsheets for the retailers, endless numbers that nobody reads. I use the AI chat tool sometimes for those reports, now that everyone else does, but I write the box copy myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most new things settle down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool for the boring jobs and that's that. I'd say it at work and to my family over Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm fine. I own my flat, thanks to help from my parents with the deposit, the mortgage is small, and I've got more than six months saved. There are plenty of brands round here if Brightwell ever let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the tool a bit more for the retailer reports, since it saves me an afternoon a month. I'd overpay the mortgage by a hundred and fifty a month, like I already do. And I'd keep helping at the community centre on Thursday evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Quite peaceful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your routine tasks would it take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The retailer reports and some of the product listings for online shops. Good riddance, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you're worried about, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's knee. My dad is a bus driver with eight years to retirement and a bad knee, and I'm the daughter who lives nearest. If he has to stop early, I'd want to help them out with money.

say: I'd say AI is a decent tool for the **boring jobs**.
I'd say the same at work and at **Sunday lunch**.
think: I'm **fine**, with my flat, a small mortgage and **six months** saved.
There are **plenty of brands** round here if needed.
do: Use the AI tool more for **retailer reports**.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** by 150 a month.
Keep volunteering at the **community centre** on Thursdays.
S0.quote: My dad is a bus driver with eight years to retirement and a bad knee, and I'm the daughter who lives nearest.
fieldNote: Her one pressure is her **father's health**, not her job.
Secure housing makes her **calm** in this picture.
**Community** and family are part of her daily life.

steps.text: Use the AI chat tool for Brightwell's monthly retailer reports
Overpay the mortgage by 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I can see that happening at Brightwell already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should learn to use the tools properly instead of fighting them. I'd also say companies owe their people some training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the team shrinks. There are six of us. Box copy, leaflets and retailer reports are what the AI tools do now. I'm average, not a star, so I could easily be one of the two who go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it working for colleagues, I'd learn the tools properly, probably the course Brightwell offers on the intranet. I'd ask to take on more of the store visits and the retailer meetings, because that's face-to-face. And I'd build the savings to a full year by cutting the holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you be thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager Sunil. He's got two little ones and a big mortgage. If the team gets cut, he's got to choose, and I don't envy him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies owe training. Do you expect the state to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather the company and my family helped. Government help always comes late and with forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's frightening, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've lost control of something important, and leaders let it happen. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is gone. I sit at a screen most of the week. Brightwell would keep a handful of people for retailer relationships, and I'm not senior enough to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the mortgage down as far as I could, so the payment is tiny. I'd take in a lodger in the second bedroom, maybe a student from the college, for extra income. And I'd apply for jobs as a store promotions lead with the electrical chains, because standing in a shop is hands-on, and robots are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be praying a lot more, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm alright because the flat is nearly paid off. That's true. But I'd stop telling my parents I can help when Dad retires, and that would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out and the new car I've been saving for. The car fund goes into the mortgage instead.

I'd say it to **anyone** who'd listen.

S2.quote: I'd stop telling my parents I can help when Dad retires, and that would hurt.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and feels it deeply.
Her biggest loss is being able to **help her parents**.
Owning her flat gives her a **floor**, which she uses well.

steps.text: Put the new car fund into paying down the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses and families need to plan for this now. I'd say it at work, and at the community centre too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it coming and that helps. I'd be 32. My writing job would still go, but I'd have time to be somewhere else first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what my colleagues do with the tools for six months, then copy what works. I'd move into retailer relationships within two years, which means talking to store buyers face to face. I'd pay the mortgage off early, and I'd look at a part-time diploma in sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait six months before learning the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of what people try with new tools doesn't work. I'd rather let the keen ones make the mistakes, then do what they got right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want to marry and have children, God willing. But I'd want the flat paid off first, so a husband and I aren't starting with debt.

I'd say it at work and at the **community centre**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given time, so we should use it well. I'd tell younger people to think hard about their degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough. I'd be 37, the flat would be paid for, and I'd have moved into something with people in it. The worry is quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the sales diploma part time over two years and move into a key account role, looking after one big retailer. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage and keep my Thursday evenings at the centre. And I'd help my cousin choose her course, because she's about to pick marketing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Layla to pick something where she meets people, or a trade. Marketing was a good choice for me ten years ago. I'm not sure it is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at Brightwell change sooner than 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reports and leaflets would go well before then, I think. But I'd be out of that work by then, if I keep to my plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to move, and I'd lose the chance to help my parents. What would help is employers being made to retrain people before cutting them, and apprenticeships for people my age in sales and trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how families share the load. In my family, if one person struggles, the rest step in. I'd want that to still be possible, not everyone on their own.

headlineQuote: In my family, if one person struggles, the rest step in.
portrait: Zoe, 27, plans campaigns for small kitchen appliances at **Brightwell Home** and loves store visits.
She owns her flat, has **six months saved**, and worries about her bus-driver dad.
In Steady Disruption she expects the **team to shrink** and learns the tools once proven.
In AGI by 2028 she'd **take a lodger** and move toward hands-on store work.
With ten years she plans a **key account** move and feels mostly fine.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she couldn't move in time or help her parents.
whatWouldHelp: Required **retraining** before cuts, and **apprenticeships** in sales and trades.
